arXiv:2011.04895v1 [math.AP] 06 Nov 2020

Blow-up and lifespan estimate for the generalized Tricomi equation with mixed nonlinearities

Makram Hamouda1 and Mohamed Ali Hamza1 Address: 1 Basic Sciences Department, Deanship of Preparatory Year and Supporting Studies, P. O. Box 1982, Imam Abdulrahman Bin Faisal University, Dammam, KSA. Email address: mmhamouda@iau.edu.sa (M. Hamouda) Email address: mahamza@iau.edu.sa (M.A. Hamza)
Abstract.

We study in this article the blow-up of the solution of the generalized Tricomi equation in the presence of two mixed nonlinearities, namely we consider

(T​r)ut​t−t2​m​Δ​u=|ut|p+|u|q,in​ℝN×[0,∞),\displaystyle(Tr)\hskip 28.45274ptu_{tt}-t^{2m}\Delta u=|u_{t}|^{p}+|u|^{q},\quad\mbox{in}\ {\mathbb{R}}^{N}\times[0,\infty),

with small initial data, where m≥0m\geq 0.
For the problem (T​r)(Tr) with m=0m=0, which corresponds to the uniform wave speed of propagation, it is known that the presence of mixed nonlinearities generates a new blow-up region in comparison with the case of a one nonlinearity (|ut|p|u_{t}|^{p} or |u|q|u|^{q}). We show in the present work that the competition between the two nonlinearities still yields a new blow region for the Tricomi equation (T​r)(Tr) with m≥0m\geq 0, and we derive an estimate of the lifespan in terms of the Tricomi parameter mm. As an application of the method developed for the study of the equation (T​r)(Tr) we obtain with a different approach the same blow-up result as in [18] when we consider only one time-derivative nonlinearity, namely we keep only |ut|p|u_{t}|^{p} in the right-hand side of (T​r)(Tr).

Key words and phrases: 
blow-up, generalized Tricomi equation, lifespan, critical curve, nonlinear wave equations, time-derivative nonlinearity.
2010 Mathematics Subject Classification
35L15, 35L71, 35B44

1. Introduction

We consider the following semilinear damped wave equation characterized by a speed of propagation of polynomial type in time, namely the well-known Generalized Tricomi wave equation with mixed nonlinearities reads as follows:

(1.1) {ut​t−t2​m​Δ​u=|ut|p+|u|q,in​ℝN×[0,∞),u(x,0)=εf(x),ut(x,0)=εg(x),x∈ℝN,\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\displaystyle u_{tt}-t^{2m}\Delta u=|u_{t}|^{p}+|u|^{q},\quad\mbox{in}\ {\mathbb{R}}^{N}\times[0,\infty),\\ u(x,0)={\varepsilon}f(x),\ u_{t}(x,0)={\varepsilon}g(x),\quad x\in{\mathbb{R}}^{N},\end{array}\right.

where m≥0m\geq 0, N≥1\ N\geq 1 denotes the space dimension, ε>0{\varepsilon}>0 is a sufficiently small parameter describing the smallness of the initial data, and f,gf,g are positive functions chosen in the energy space with compact support. Moreover, the functions ff and gg are supposed to be positive and compactly supported on BℝN​(0,R),R>0B_{{\mathbb{R}}^{N}}(0,R),R>0.

Throughout this article, we assume that m≥0m\geq 0, p,q>1p,q>1 and q≤2​NN−2q\leq\frac{2N}{N-2} if N≥3N\geq 3.

The study of the Cauchy problem (1.1) has been taking different considerations depending on the choice of the nonlinear terms. Being not at all exhaustive, we will recall in the following some existing works in the literature in this direction. Let us first rewrite the system (1.1) in a more general context. More precisely, we consider the following family of semilinear wave equations:

(1.2) {ut​t−t2​m​Δ​u=a​|ut|p+b​|u|q,in​ℝN×[0,∞),u(x,0)=εf(x),ut(x,0)=εg(x),x∈ℝN,\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\displaystyle u_{tt}-t^{2m}\Delta u=a|u_{t}|^{p}+b|u|^{q},\quad\mbox{in}\ {\mathbb{R}}^{N}\times[0,\infty),\\ u(x,0)={\varepsilon}f(x),\ u_{t}(x,0)={\varepsilon}g(x),\quad x\in{\mathbb{R}}^{N},\end{array}\right.

where aa and bb are two nonnegative constants.

Let (a,b)=(0,1)(a,b)=(0,1) and m=0m=0 in (1.2). It is worth mentioning that the obtained system was subject to several works and the related blow-up phenomenon is more or less well understood and is linked to the Strauss conjecture. More precisely, this case involves the critical power, qSq_{S}, which is the positive root of the quadratic equation (N−1)​q2−(N+1)​q−2=0(N-1)q^{2}-(N+1)q-2=0, and is given by

(1.3) qS=qS​(N):=N+1+N2+10​N−72​(N−1).q_{S}=q_{S}(N):=\frac{N+1+\sqrt{N^{2}+10N-7}}{2(N-1)}.

Indeed, if q≤qSq\leq q_{S} then no global solution for (1.2) does exist (under some assumptions on the initial data), and for q>qSq>q_{S} a global solution exists for small initial data; see e.g. [17, 22, 26, 27].

Now, the case m=0m=0 and (a,b)=(1,0)(a,b)=(1,0) is connected with the Glassey conjecture saying that the critical power pGp_{G} should be given by

(1.4) pG=pG​(N):=1+2N−1.p_{G}=p_{G}(N):=1+\frac{2}{N-1}.

The critical value pGp_{G} generates two regions for the power pp; one stating the global existence (for p>pGp>p_{G}) and another one for the nonexistence (for p≤pGp\leq p_{G}) of a global small data solution; see e.g. [12, 14, 16, 21, 24, 28].

The case m=0m=0 and a,b≠0a,b\neq 0 (we may assume that (a,b)=(1,1)(a,b)=(1,1)) is characterized by two mixed nonlinearities. In this case, and having p≤pGp\leq p_{G} or q≤qSq\leq q_{S}, the blow-up of the solution of (1.2) is easy. However, compared to a one single nonlinearity, the presence of mixed nonlinearities produces a supplementary blow-up region. In fact, for p>pGp>p_{G} and q>qSq>q_{S}, the new blow-up frontier is characterized by the following relationship between pp and qq:

(1.5) λ⁡(p,q,N):=(q−1)​[(N−1)​p−2]<4;\lambda(p,q,N):=(q-1)\big[(N-1)p-2\big]<4;

see e.g. [1, 7, 13, 25] for more details.

Now, let us consider m≥0m\geq 0 and (a,b)=(0,1)(a,b)=(0,1) in (1.2). This case corresponds to the semilinear generalized Tricomi equation with power nonlinearity which has been widely studied in several works. In [9, 19], the authors proved the blow-up results for both the subcritical and critical cases. However, the question of global existence for the system (1.2) with small data in the supercritical case has been proved only for m=1m=1 and for dimensions N=1,2N=1,2; see e.g. [8, 9, 10, 11]. Hence, the critical exponent for (1.2), that we denote by qC​(N,m)q_{C}(N,m), should be given by the greatest root of the following quadratic equation

(1.6) 𝒬t​r​(q):=((m+1)​N−1)​q2−((m+1)​N+1−2​m)​q−2​(m+1)=0.\displaystyle\mathcal{Q}_{tr}(q):=((m+1)N-1)q^{2}-((m+1)N+1-2m)q-2(m+1)=0.

Naturally, for m=0m=0 we find again the well-known Strauss exponent qS​(N)q_{S}(N), namely qC​(N,0)=qS​(N)q_{C}(N,0)=q_{S}(N), where qS​(N)q_{S}(N) is given by (1.3).

For m≥0m\geq 0 and (a,b)=(1,0)(a,b)=(1,0), the system (1.2) is given by

(1.7) {ut​t−t2​m​Δ​u=|ut|p,in​ℝN×[0,∞),u(x,0)=εf(x),ut(x,0)=εg(x),x∈ℝN.\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\displaystyle u_{tt}-t^{2m}\Delta u=|u_{t}|^{p},\quad\mbox{in}\ {\mathbb{R}}^{N}\times[0,\infty),\\ u(x,0)={\varepsilon}f(x),\ u_{t}(x,0)={\varepsilon}g(x),\quad x\in{\mathbb{R}}^{N}.\end{array}\right.

Concerning the blow-up results and lifespan estimate of the solution of (1.7), it was proven in [20] that for p≤pG​(N⁡(m+1))p\leq p_{G}(N(m+1)) we have the blow-up. To prove this result, the authors used, among other tools, the integral representation formula in one space dimension. However, this result was recently improved in [18]. The main tool in the latter work is the construction of adequate test functions using the properties of Bessel functions. Hence, the new obtained region involves an almost sure candidate for the critical exponent, that is

(1.8) p≤pt​r​(N,m):=1+2(m+1)​(N−1)−m.p\leq p_{tr}(N,m):=1+\frac{2}{(m+1)(N-1)-m}.

The authors in [18] conjecture that pt​r​(N,m)p_{tr}(N,m) is in fact the critical exponent for the blow-up of the solution of (1.7). Of course this has to be confirmed by a global existence result for (1.7).

We are interested in this article in studying the blow-up result of the solution of (1.1) for m≥0m\geq 0. First, let us recall that the case m=0m=0 in (1.1) corresponds in fact to the classical wave equation with mixed nonlinearities which, compared to the case with one nonlinearity |ut|p|u_{t}|^{p} or |u|q|u|^{q}, for p>pG​(N)p>p_{G}(N) or q>qS​(N)q>q_{S}(N), generates a new blow-up region, given by (1.5), due to the interaction between the two mixed nonlinearities. In this work we will examine the influence of the parameter mm on the blow-up result and the lifespan estimate for the Cauchy problem (1.1) for m≥0m\geq 0. Naturally, the emphasis will be here for the exponents p>pt​r​(N,m)p>p_{tr}(N,m) or q>qC​(N,m)q>q_{C}(N,m). Our target is to give the curve delimiting the new blow-up region for the Tricomi equation given by (1.1), and to look into its change compared to (1.5).

The Tricomi equation constitutes somehow a time-dependent wave speed of propagation. As shown below (see (1.10)), the effect of this Tricomi term is more or less similar to a scale-invariant damping. For instance, let v⁡(x,τ)=u⁡(x,t)v(x,\tau)=u(x,t) where

(1.9) τ=ξ⁡(t):=tm+1m+1.\tau=\xi(t):=\frac{t^{m+1}}{m+1}.

Hence, the solution v⁡(x,τ)v(x,\tau) verifies the following equation:

(1.10) vτ​τ−Δ​v+μmτ​∂τv=Cm,p​τμm​(p−2)​|∂τv|p+𝒦m​τ−2​μm​|v|q,in​ℝN×[0,∞),\displaystyle v_{\tau\tau}-\Delta v+\frac{\mu_{m}}{\tau}\,\partial_{\tau}v=C_{m,p}\tau^{\mu_{m}(p-2)}|\partial_{\tau}v|^{p}+\mathcal{K}_{m}\tau^{-2\mu_{m}}|v|^{q},\quad\mbox{in}\ {\mathbb{R}}^{N}\times[0,\infty),

where μm:=mm+1\mu_{m}:=\frac{m}{m+1}, 𝒦m=(m+1)−2​μm\mathcal{K}_{m}=(m+1)^{-2\mu_{m}} and Cm,p=(m+1)μm​(p−2)C_{m,p}=(m+1)^{\mu_{m}(p-2)}. Note that the equation (1.10) is somehow related to the Euler-Darboux-Poisson equation. Moreover, thanks to this transformation, which implies a kind of similarity with the scale-invariant damping case, we can inherit the methods used in our previous works [4, 5, 6] to build the proofs of our main results which are related, as a first target, to the blow-up of the solution of (1.1) and, as a secondary aim, to the blow-up of (1.7).

The article is organized as follows. The beginning of Section 2 is devoted to the setting of the weak formulation of (1.1) in the energy space. Then, we state the main theorems of our work, and we end this section by some remarks. To develop the proofs of our results, we prove some technical lemmas in Section 3. Finally, Sections 4 and 5 are committed to the proofs of Theorems 2.2 and 2.3.

2. Main Results

In this section, we start by giving a sense to the energy solution of (1.1) which reads as follows:

Definition 2.1.

Let f,g∈𝒞0∞​(ℝN)f,g\in\mathcal{C}_{0}^{\infty}({\mathbb{R}}^{N}). We say that uu is an energy solution of (1.1) on [0,T)[0,T) if

{u∈𝒞⁡([0,T),H1​(ℝN))∩𝒞1​([0,T),L2​(ℝN)),u∈Ll​o​cq​((0,T)×ℝN)​and​ut∈Ll​o​cp​((0,T)×ℝN),\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}u\in\mathcal{C}([0,T),H^{1}({\mathbb{R}}^{N}))\cap\mathcal{C}^{1}([0,T),L^{2}({\mathbb{R}}^{N})),\\ u\in L^{q}_{loc}((0,T)\times{\mathbb{R}}^{N})\ \text{and}\ u_{t}\in L^{p}_{loc}((0,T)\times{\mathbb{R}}^{N}),\end{array}\right.

satisfies, for all Φ∈𝒞0∞​(ℝN×[0,T))\Phi\in\mathcal{C}_{0}^{\infty}({\mathbb{R}}^{N}\times[0,T)) and all t∈[0,T)t\in[0,T), the following equation:

(2.1) ∫ℝNut​(x,t)​Φ​(x,t)​𝑑x−∫ℝNut​(x,0)​Φ​(x,0)​𝑑x−∫0t∫ℝNut(x,s)Φt(x,s)dxds+∫0ts2​m∫ℝN∇u(x,s)⋅∇Φ(x,s)dxds=∫0t∫ℝN{|ut​(x,s)|p+|u⁡(x,s)|q}​Φ​(x,s)​dx​ds.\begin{array}[]{l}\displaystyle\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{N}}u_{t}(x,t)\Phi(x,t)dx-\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{N}}u_{t}(x,0)\Phi(x,0)dx\\ \displaystyle-\int_{0}^{t}\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{N}}u_{t}(x,s)\Phi_{t}(x,s)dx\,ds+\int_{0}^{t}s^{2m}\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{N}}\nabla u(x,s)\cdot\nabla\Phi(x,s)dx\,ds\\ \displaystyle=\int_{0}^{t}\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{N}}\left\{|u_{t}(x,s)|^{p}+|u(x,s)|^{q}\right\}\Phi(x,s)dx\,ds.\end{array}

It is clear that the weak formulation corresponding to (1.7) is also given by an analogous identity to (2.1) with omitting the nonlinear term |u|q|u|^{q}.

Now, we state the main results of this article which are related to the blow-up region and the lifespan estimate of the solutions of (1.1) and (1.7), respectively.

Theorem 2.2.

Let p,q>1p,q>1 and m≥0m\geq 0 such that

(2.2) Λ⁡(p,q,N,m)<4,\Lambda(p,q,N,m)<4,

where Λ⁡(p,q,N,m)\Lambda(p,q,N,m) is defined by

(2.3) Λ⁡(p,q,N,m):=(q−1)​[(m+1)​(N−1)​p−m⁡(p−2)−2],\Lambda(p,q,N,m):=(q-1)\big[(m+1)(N-1)p-m(p-2)-2\big],

and p>pt​r​(N,m)p>p_{tr}(N,m) and q>qC​(N,m)q>q_{C}(N,m).
Suppose that f,g∈𝒞0∞​(ℝN)f,g\in\mathcal{C}_{0}^{\infty}({\mathbb{R}}^{N}) are non-negative functions which are compactly supported on BℝN​(0,R)B_{{\mathbb{R}}^{N}}(0,R), and do not vanish everywhere. Let uu be an energy solution of (1.1) on [0,Tε)[0,T_{\varepsilon}) (in the sense of (2.1)) such that supp​(u)⊂{(x,t)∈ℝN×[0,∞):|x|≤ξ⁡(t)+R}\mbox{\rm supp}(u)\ \subset\{(x,t)\in{\mathbb{R}}^{N}\times[0,\infty):|x|\leq\xi(t)+R\}. Then, there exists a constant ε0=ε0​(f,g,N,R,p,q,m)>0{\varepsilon}_{0}={\varepsilon}_{0}(f,g,N,R,p,q,m)>0 such that TεT_{\varepsilon} verifies

Tε≤C​ε−2​p​(q−1)4−Λ⁡(p,q,N,m),T_{\varepsilon}\leq C\,{\varepsilon}^{-\frac{2p(q-1)}{4-\Lambda(p,q,N,m)}},

where CC is a positive constant independent of ε{\varepsilon} and 0<ε≤ε00<{\varepsilon}\leq{\varepsilon}_{0}.

Theorem 2.3.

Let p>1p>1 and m≥0m\geq 0. Assume that the initial data ff and gg verify the same hypotheses as in Theorem 2.2. Then, for uu an energy solution of (1.7) on [0,Tε)[0,T_{\varepsilon}) which satisfies supp​(u)⊂{(x,t)∈ℝN×[0,∞):|x|≤ξ⁡(t)+R}\mbox{\rm supp}(u)\ \subset\{(x,t)\in{\mathbb{R}}^{N}\times[0,\infty):|x|\leq\xi(t)+R\}, there exists a constant ε0=ε0​(f,g,N,R,p,m)>0{\varepsilon}_{0}={\varepsilon}_{0}(f,g,N,R,p,m)>0 such that TεT_{\varepsilon} verifies

Tε≤{C​ε−2​(p−1)2−((m+1)​(N−1)−m)​(p−1)for​ 1<p<pt​r​(N,m),exp⁡(C​ε−(p−1))for​p=pt​r​(N,m)=1+2(m+1)​(N−1)−m,T_{\varepsilon}\leq\displaystyle\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}C\,{\varepsilon}^{-\frac{2(p-1)}{2-((m+1)(N-1)-m)(p-1)}}&\ \text{for}\ 1<p<p_{tr}(N,m),\\ \exp\left(C{\varepsilon}^{-(p-1)}\right)&\ \text{for}\ p=p_{tr}(N,m)=1+\frac{2}{(m+1)(N-1)-m},\end{array}\right.

where CC is a positive constant independent of ε{\varepsilon} and 0<ε≤ε00<{\varepsilon}\leq{\varepsilon}_{0}.

Remark 2.1.

Note that for m=0m=0 in (1.1), we have Λ⁡(p,q,N,0)=λ⁡(p,q,N)\Lambda(p,q,N,0)=\lambda(p,q,N), which are respectively given by (2.3) and (1.5), and this gives raise to the classical wave equation with combined nonlinearities.

Remark 2.2.

Let

p0:=pt​r​(N,m)+β1=1+2(m+1)​(N−1)−m+β1,p_{0}:=p_{tr}(N,m)+\beta_{1}=1+\frac{2}{(m+1)(N-1)-m}+\beta_{1},

and

q0:=1+4(m+1)​(N−1)​p0−m⁡(p0−2)−2−β2>1+4(m+1)​N−1−β3,\displaystyle q_{0}:=1+\frac{4}{(m+1)(N-1)p_{0}-m(p_{0}-2)-2}-\beta_{2}>1+\frac{4}{(m+1)N-1}-\beta_{3},

where βi\beta_{i} is a positive constant taken small enough for all i=1,2,3i=1,2,3.
It is easy to see that 𝒬t​r​(1+4(m+1)​N−1)>0\mathcal{Q}_{tr}\left(1+\frac{4}{(m+1)N-1}\right)>0. Then, for β1\beta_{1} and β2\beta_{2} small enough, we have 𝒬t​r​(q0)>0\mathcal{Q}_{tr}(q_{0})>0. Consequently, we have q0>qC​(N,m)q_{0}>q_{C}(N,m) for β1\beta_{1} and β2\beta_{2} small enough. Hence, the pair (p0,q0)(p_{0},q_{0}) satisfies (2.2), p0>pt​r​(N,m)p_{0}>p_{tr}(N,m) and q0>qC​(N,m)q_{0}>q_{C}(N,m). Hence, the hypothesis on pp and qq in Theorem 2.2 makes sense.

Remark 2.3.

We note that, for p>pG​(N)p>p_{G}(N) and q>qS​(N)q>q_{S}(N), the equality in (1.5) yields the global existence of the solution of (1.2) (with m=0m=0 and (a,b)=(1,1)(a,b)=(1,1)) without the intermediate step of “almost global solution”; see [13]. This is in fact related to the presence of mixed nonlinearities. Naturally, it is interesting to see whether this phenomenon still occurs for the case m>0m>0, namely when Λ⁡(p,q,N,m)=4\Lambda(p,q,N,m)=4 and for p>pt​r​(N,m)p>p_{tr}(N,m) and q>qC​(N,m)q>q_{C}(N,m). To complete the whole picture, the global existence in-time of the solution of (1.1) will be studied in a subsequent work.

where ϕ⁡(x)\phi(x) is introduced in [26], and ρ⁡(t)\rho(t) verifies

Along this work, we will denote by CC any positive constant which may depend on the data (p,q,m,N,R,f,gp,q,m,N,R,f,g) but not on ε\varepsilon and whose value may change from line to line. However, in some occurrences, we will make precise the dependence of the constant CC on the parameters of the problem.

The following lemma holds true for the function ψ⁡(x,t)\psi(x,t).

Remark 3.1.

Note that the same conclusions as in Lemmas 3.2 and 3.3 can be obtained for any positive nonlinearity of the form F⁡(u,ut)F(u,u_{t}) instead of |ut|p+|u|q|u_{t}|^{p}+|u|^{q}. Indeed, in the proofs of these lemmas we only used the non negativity of the nonlinearities |ut|p|u_{t}|^{p} and |u|q|u|^{q}. Moreover, the results of Lemmas 3.2 and 3.3 naturally hold true for a one nonlinearity |ut|p|u_{t}|^{p} or |u|q|u|^{q} as it is the case for (1.7).

5. Proof of Theorem 2.3.

The purpose of this section is to give the details on the proof of Theorem 2.3 which is related to the solution of (1.7). For that aim, we use the computations already obtained in Section 3 . First, we note that Lemmas 3.2 and 3.3 remain true for the solution of (1.7) instead of (1.1) (see Remark 3.1) since we only used the non negativity of the nonlinear terms and not their types.

In fact, the result in this section is somehow an application (and does not constitute in any case the main objective of this work) of the result obtained for problem (1.1) with mixed nonlinearities in Theorem 2.2. Indeed, we note here that the blow-up result for the system (1.7) is also obtained in [18]; the result there is the same as in Theorem 2.3. However, our approach here is totally different. Moreover, we believe that our method can be used to study the blow-up of the system with generalized Tricomi term. This will be the subject of a forthcoming work.

In order to prove the blow-up result for (1.7) we will use the estimate (3.35) (initially proved for (1.1)) with omitting the nonlinear term |u⁡(x,t)|q|u(x,t)|^{q}. Hence, the analogous of the estimate (3.35) reads as follows:

Now, we introduce the following functional:

where C4=min⁡(Cm​(f,g)/4,8​CG2)C_{4}=\min(C_{m}(f,g)/4,8C_{G_{2}}) (CG2C_{G_{2}} is defined in Lemma 3.3) and T~3>T1\tilde{T}_{3}>T_{1} is chosen such that tm4−3​Γ​(t)32>0\frac{t^{m}}{4}-\frac{3\Gamma(t)}{32}>0 for all t≥T~3t\geq\tilde{T}_{3} (this is possible thanks to (3.19) and (3.9)).
Let

ℱ⁡(t):=G2​(t)−H⁡(t),\mathcal{F}(t):=G_{2}(t)-H(t),

(5.2) ℱ′​(t)+3​Γ​(t)4​ℱ​(t)≥(tm4−3​Γ​(t)32)​∫T~4t∫ℝN|ut​(x,s)|p​ψ​(x,s)​𝑑x​𝑑s+78​∫ℝN|ut​(x,t)|p​ψ​(x,t)​𝑑x+C4​(tm−3​Γ​(t)32)​ε≥0,∀t≥T~3.\begin{array}[]{rcl}\displaystyle\mathcal{F}^{\prime}(t)+\frac{3\Gamma(t)}{4}\mathcal{F}(t)&\geq&\displaystyle\left(\frac{t^{m}}{4}-\frac{3\Gamma(t)}{32}\right)\int_{\tilde{T}_{4}}^{t}\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{N}}|u_{t}(x,s)|^{p}\psi(x,s)dxds\\ &+&\displaystyle\frac{7}{8}\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{N}}|u_{t}(x,t)|^{p}\psi(x,t)dx+C_{4}\left(t^{m}-\frac{3\Gamma(t)}{32}\right){\varepsilon}\\ &\geq&0,\quad\forall\ t\geq\tilde{T}_{3}.\end{array}

The appendix is aimed to give some light on the property (iii) in Section 3, namely (3.9), of the function ρ⁡(t)\rho(t), the solution of (3.2), by showing some elementary results on the behavior of ρ⁡(t)\rho(t) for tt large enough. Hence, we first rewrite the expression of ρ⁡(t)\rho(t) as follows:

(6.1) ρ⁡(t)={αm​t12​K12​m+2​(ξ⁡(t)),∀t>0,1,at​t=0,\rho(t)=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\displaystyle\alpha_{m}t^{\frac{1}{2}}K_{\frac{1}{2m+2}}\left(\xi(t)\right),&\quad\forall\ t>0,\\ 1,&\quad\text{at}\ t=0,\end{array}\right.

where

Kν​(z)=∫0∞exp⁡(−z​cosh⁡ζ)​cosh⁡(ν​ζ)​𝑑ζ,ν∈ℝ.K_{\nu}(z)=\int_{0}^{\infty}\exp(-z\cosh\zeta)\cosh(\nu\zeta)d\zeta,\ \nu\in\mathbb{R}.

Using the fact that

(6.2) dd​z​Kν​(z)=−Kν+1​(z)+νz​Kν​(z),\frac{d}{dz}K_{\nu}(z)=-K_{\nu+1}(z)+\frac{\nu}{z}K_{\nu}(z),

we infer that

(6.3) ρ′​(t)ρ⁡(t)=1t−K2​m+32​m+2​(ξ​(t))K12​m+2​(ξ​(t))​tm,∀t>0.\frac{\rho^{\prime}(t)}{\rho(t)}=\frac{1}{t}-\frac{K_{\frac{2m+3}{2m+2}}(\xi(t))}{K_{\frac{1}{2m+2}}(\xi(t))}t^{m},\quad\forall\ t>0.

From [3], we have the following property of the function Kμ​(t)K_{\mu}(t):

(6.4) Kν(t)=π2​te−t(1+O(t−1),ast→∞.K_{\nu}(t)=\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{2t}}e^{-t}(1+O(t^{-1}),\quad\text{as}\ t\to\infty.

Combining (6.3) and (6.4), we deduce the property (3.9).
